statement: Planned single-run distance and duration should not exceed 1.10 x the longest completed run of the trailing 30 days in that dimension; runs above this are flagged and the generator plans at or below it. No study supports a different threshold.
unit: ratio (planned / longest completed run in the last 30 days)
appliesTo: All runners, novice and experienced alike; for runners with no recent logs, the declared longest recent run

statement: Warn when a planned or logged run is more than 10% above the 30-day longest run (observed HRR about 1.5-1.6), and treat more than 2.0x as the highest-risk band (HRR about 2.3) that the generator never schedules without an explicit override. Do not describe the 30-100% band as safer than 10-30%. Describe all bands as observed associations, not causal limits.

Check each long-run step against the rolling 30-day maximum of completed runs, not planned runs or weekly volume. A completed race of marathon distance or longer (42.195 km or more) does not count toward the 30-day reference, in the check and in the generator alike; shorter races count as runs. The window is grade B; the race exclusion is grade D, because a race effort sets a reference that no training run should follow.
value: 30 days; races of 42.195 km or more excluded

statement: Keep the 30-day reference window for the session guard; no study compares windows, and the calculation method changes which sessions are flagged (16-33% of sessions at the same cutoffs). Every ramp and spike rule states its window, and the weekly ramp compares a week with the highest of the 2 preceding loading weeks so a week after a recovery, taper or race week is not read as a jump.
value: 30-day session window; weekly baseline = max of 2 preceding loading weeks

statement: Apply the session guard to distance (grade B) and to duration (grade D: a duration-based load ratio was associated with injury in a second GPS cohort, adjusted HR 1.33, but that cohort measured an ACWR-type ratio and the association vanished once runners injured at baseline were excluded, so it is indirect support only), and to per-session gain and descent against their own 30-day maxima with a 100 m minimum step (grade D, no evidence in road or trail studies). Do not combine pace and volume into one threshold.
value: 1.10 on distance, duration, gain and descent; 100 m minimum step for gain and descent
appliesTo: All runners; gain and descent mainly trail and ultra

statement: When the longest recent run is short, allow a minimum absolute step so the 10% rule stays usable. The number is an engineering default and is shown as one.
appliesTo: Runners whose longest 30-day run is under about 5 km

statement: Default weekly volume ramp is 10% as a soft default that gives a warning when exceeded. The 10% number is a convention that matches published plans (5-9% average build) and has no evidence as an injury threshold; the only RCT of a 10%-rule programme found no effect. Label it a default.

Hard ceiling of 30% growth over any 2-week window. Weak cohort signals sit in this region (more injury after a 20-60% weekly increase at one time point; injured novices' pre-injury week +86% while uninjured novices averaged +22%; non-significant distance-injury signal above 30%). Neither a tighter (20%/week) nor a looser ceiling is supported.

User-facing copy never says that the 10% rule or any progression limit prevents injury or that exceeding a limit causes injury; limits are conservative defaults, the session guard is an observed association, and the app does not compute a personal injury probability.

Do not use ACWR (any window, EWMA or rolling) or the week-to-week ratio as a constraint, objective, risk score or safety claim. The largest running cohort found an inverse ACWR association, and a second GPS cohort's small association disappeared when runners injured at baseline were excluded.
If an ACWR is displayed, it is descriptive only, with no sweet-spot band, hidden in taper and recovery weeks, and shown only after a 4-week warm-up (engineering default).

Collect injury history at onboarding and mark runners with a recent injury as higher risk; the flag selects the conservative profile. The flag is true for any injury listed in the profile for the last 12 months, running-related or not, because the profile records no running-related field. Previous injury is the best-supported risk factor across reviews and in a Couch-to-5k cohort.
value: true if any injury is listed in the profile for the last 12 months, running-related or not (window is an engineering choice)

statement: For flagged runners: the 1.10x session limit is hard (no override), weekly ramp 5-7%, recovery week every 3rd week. The factor is well supported; these values are unvalidated defaults.
value: session cap 1.10 hard; ramp 0.05-0.07; recovery every 3rd week

statement: A previous bone stress injury triggers the most conservative profile, a clinician prompt and a gradual return; menstrual irregularity triggers a medical-review caution, not a plan parameter.
value: hard session cap 1.10; ramp <= 0.05; clinician prompt
appliesTo: Runners with previous BSI or reported menstrual irregularity

statement: No sex-specific volume or progression cap; sex only adjusts injury-specific cautions (bone stress and energy availability for women, Achilles for men).

Runners the engine classifies as novice get the conservative defaults: 10% soft ramp, 1.10x session guard, time-based progression and 2:1 recovery cadence. The per-hour injury rate is about 2.3x that of recreational runners, and no previous experience and low volume are risk factors; no study supports a stricter or looser novice step size.
value: ramp <= 0.10; session cap 1.10; recovery every 3rd week

statement: Do not loosen the session guard or weekly ramp for experienced runners: runners with more than 40 years of running had more injuries, more experience was associated with injury in trail runners, and competitive runners had the highest pooled incidence.
value: same G-1 and G-2 for all experience classes

statement: A runner whose logged frequency averages under 2 runs per week over the last 4 weeks gets the novice ramp handling and 2:1 recovery cadence, whatever experience they report. The marker comes from a large cohort; the cutoff use and the 4-week window are engineering defaults.
appliesTo: Runners not otherwise classified as novice

statement: Couch-to-5k style starter plans are a convention without an evidence base. A returner with a continuous run of 20 min or more in the last 30 days takes 3 sessions of N min, N being that run rounded down to 5 min and clamped between 20 and 30; N above 20 needs at least 2 years of running, no soft flag and no recent-injury flag, so a session never exceeds the runner's own completed run. Other runners start on the run-walk ladder. The runner can repeat a week or pause without penalty, and a week advances only after at least 80% of it was completed with no pain.
value: 3 x clamp(30-day longest run, 20, 30) min; repeat week allowed
appliesTo: Novice and returning runners starting at the restart floor

statement: Do not add a combined pace-and-volume progression threshold: the interaction of weekly volume and pace progression was not significant (wide CIs). Intensity progression stays governed separately (one lever at a time).
Symptom or niggle check-ins are a secondary signal; most overuse injuries have no reported preceding problem, so check-ins never replace load guards or act as injury prediction.
unit: proportion of overuse injuries with a prior problem

statement: For ultra, trail and multi-day preparation, apply the same session guard on distance, duration, gain and descent, label it an unvalidated extrapolation, and allow explicit override; no trail or ultra study tests load progression or elevation as a risk factor.
value: 1.10 on distance, duration, gain and descent; unvalidated
appliesTo: Runners training for ultra or trail events
